verification.note: Unit 11 (d and f Block Elements) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 8 ("8. d & f BLOCK ELEMENTS"), book pp.91-94, which prints this question on book p.92 as VSAQ 12. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK ANSWER KEPT AND COMPLETED (book p.92, VSAQ 12): the printed definition and the printed three-way split into positive, negative and neutral species are both correct, but the book gives examples of neutral and negative ligands only (NH₃, H₂O, Cl⁻) and none of a positive one, even though it lists the type. The card supplies NO⁺ and the hydrazinium ion NH₂–NH₃⁺. It also names the word LONE pair, which the book omits — a ligand donates a lone pair, which is why CH₄ with no lone pair is not a ligand.

d and f Block Elements — 2 marks

steps.label: Definition
lines: A ligand is an ion or a molecule that
donates a lone pair of electrons to a
The bond formed is a coordinate covalent
bond, with both electrons supplied by
The atom of the ligand that donates the

steps.why: Every ligand needs at least one lone pair, and that is why NH₃, H₂O and Cl⁻ are ligands while CH₄ is not. The metal supplies an empty orbital and the ligand supplies both electrons, which is what makes the bond coordinate rather than ordinary covalent.
common_mistakes: Saying the metal donates the electron pair. The ligand donates it and the metal accepts it.
Calling CH₄ a ligand. It has no lone pair, so it has no donor atom.
steps.memory_tip: Ligand = lone pair donor. Metal = lone pair acceptor.
steps.margin_note: The words lone pair and coordinate covalent bond are the two marked terms.

steps.label: Types with examples
lines: A ligand may be negative, neutral or

lines.text: Every ligand is a Lewis base

lines: and the metal ion is the Lewis acid.
steps.why: Positive ligands are uncommon but real, and naming one shows the definition has been understood rather than copied, because a positive ion still has a lone pair to donate. Calling the ligand a Lewis base and the metal a Lewis acid states the same idea in the language of acids and bases used in the chemical bonding chapter.
common_mistakes: Giving neutral examples only. One example from each of the three types is what completes this mark.
Writing Na⁺ as a ligand. Na⁺ has no lone pair to donate.
steps.memory_tip: Three kinds: negative such as Cl⁻, neutral such as NH₃, positive such as NO⁺.
steps.margin_note: Two or three examples are enough. Naming a positive ligand is the part most answers leave out.

insider_note: A one-line definition is one mark. The second mark comes from examples that cover more than one charge type, so give a negative one and a neutral one at the least.
